VIDEO.title: Why Did Jesus Offer a Cup Instead of a Throne?
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

kicker: Study aid · Matthew 20:17-34 · Episode 40 (#43 of 58 in the playlist)
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 20:17-34. On the road up to Jerusalem Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them, for the third time, that the Son of Man will be handed to the chief priests and scribes, condemned, handed to the Gentiles to be mocked, flogged and crucified, and raised on the third day. Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee kneels and asks that her two sons sit at His right and left in His kingdom. Jesus asks them whether they can drink His cup; they say they can. The ten are indignant, and Jesus teaches that the great among them must be servants, as the Son of Man came to serve and give His life a ransom for many. Leaving Jericho, He opens the eyes of two blind men who cry out, 'Son of David.'

Jesus has been travelling toward Jerusalem since 19:1. 'Chief priests and scribes' with the power to condemn points to the Sanhedrin, which then handed people to Rome for execution. Jesus speaks of His death as 'the Son of Man,' the figure of Daniel 7:13-14.

The mother speaks, but Jesus answers the sons, who answer back: they had put her up to it. The video suggests she may have been Mary's sister, which would make James and John Jesus' cousins. The cup in Scripture means both God's wrath (Jeremiah 25:15; Isaiah 51:17; Matthew 26:39) and one's God-given portion (Psalm 16:5). Only Jesus drinks the cup of wrath, but James (Acts 12:2) and John (Revelation 1:9) will share His suffering.

Daniel saw the Son of Man receive dominion, never suffer, which probably confused the disciples. Isaiah 52-53 supplies the rest: the servant despised, pierced and bearing the sin of many, behind 'a ransom for many.' Matthew sets two blind men right after two 'blind' disciples, and Jesus asks both the same question: what do you want?
The lesson: greatness in the kingdom of God is not based on the world's model of self-aggrandizement, but on Jesus' model of self-sacrifice. The cup before the crown, the cross before the throne.
QUOTES: The cup before the crown, the cross before the throne.
Greatness in the kingdom of God is not based on the world's model of self-aggrandizement, but on Jesus' model of self-sacrifice.
The cup that a Christian drinks will not be made of the world's gold, but of Christ's suffering.
Ascension and glorification comes after descension. That's the order.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?
just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many.
Yahweh is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; / You support my lot.

src.text: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem; and the Son of Man will be betrayed to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn Him to death, and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles to mock and flog and crucify Him, and on the third day He will be raised up.”

lines.text: Jesus has been travelling to Jerusalem since 19:1. The teaching on divorce, the rich ruler and the vineyard parable all happen on the way.
He knows how He will die, down to the mocking, flogging and crucifixion, and when He will rise. How did He know? A good student should ask, and look to the Old Testament.
This is the third prediction in Matthew (16:21; 17:22-23), and the first to name crucifixion and the Gentiles.

left.text: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem; and the Son of Man will be betrayed to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn Him to death,

right.text: So Pilate said to them, “Take Him yourselves, and judge Him according to your law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death,”

lines.text: The pairing of both kinds of leaders, and the power to condemn to death, point to the Sanhedrin. Rome did not let it carry out executions, so it would sentence people and hand them over to the Romans, which is what happens to Jesus.

src.text: “I kept looking in the night visions, / And behold, with the clouds of heaven / One like a Son of Man was coming, / And He came up to the Ancient of Days / And came near before Him. / And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed.

lines.text: Jesus does not say 'I will die' in 20:18; He uses 'the Son of Man,' pointing to Old Testament prophecy about the Messiah. None of this should have surprised the disciples.
Other texts outside the Bible, including 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra, probably shaped expectations too. But Daniel never saw the Son of Man suffer and die, and that probably confused the disciples.

src.text: He was despised and forsaken of men, / A man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; / And like one from whom men hide their face / He was despised, and we did not esteem Him. / Surely our griefs He Himself bore, / And our sorrows He carried; / Yet we ourselves esteemed Him stricken, / Smitten of God, and afflicted. / But He was pierced through for our transgressions, / He was crushed for our iniquities; / The chastening for our peace fell upon Him, / And by His wounds we are healed.

lines.text: Where does Jesus get the mocking and flogging? From Isaiah 52 and 53, where the servant is oppressed, afflicted, pierced, His appearance marred more than any man (52:14; 53:7).
The disciples should have known Daniel 7 and Isaiah 52-53. It seems they missed these hints.

left.text: And He said to her, “What do you wish?” She *said to Him, “Command that in Your kingdom these two sons of mine may sit one on Your right and one on Your left.”

right.text: But Jesus answered and said, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They *said to Him, “We are able.”

lines.text: She asks, but Jesus does not answer her. He speaks straight to James and John, and they answer Him. They had put their mother up to it.
Mark 10:35-37 tells it with James and John making the request themselves.

src.text: Among them was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee.

lines.text: Comparing the women at the cross, she could have been Mary's sister, Jesus' aunt. That would make James and John His cousins, and her appeal makes more sense: she wants His family to have royal recognition.
Mark names Salome at the cross (Mark 15:40); John names His mother's sister (John 19:25). Whether these are the same woman is an inference, not stated.

left.text: For thus Yahweh, the God of Israel, says to me, “Take this cup of the wine of wrath from My hand and cause all the nations to whom I send you to drink it.

right.text: And He went a little beyond them, and fell on His face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; yet not as I will, but as You will.”

lines.text: The cup is a common picture of suffering, especially the suffering caused by God's wrath. Isaiah 51:17 speaks of Jerusalem drinking the cup of His wrath, and Jesus will pray in Gethsemane for this cup to pass.
So the rhetorical answer to 'Are you able?' is no: only Jesus can drink the cup of God's wrath and take on the sins of the whole world.

left.text: Yahweh is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; / You support my lot.

right.text: He *said to them, “My cup you shall drink; but to sit on My right and on My left, this is not Mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by My Father.”

lines.text: The cup is also a person's God-given portion or destiny. In that sense Jesus can say 'My cup you shall drink': they will share His rejection, persecution and self-denial, and His obedience unto glory.
And He was right. James is killed by Herod (Acts 12:2) and John suffers exile on Patmos (Revelation 1:9).
Jesus is a servant of the Father's will; all authority is given to Him later (28:18). As He yields to the Father, James and John should let go of their desire for authority.

src.text: But Jesus called them to Himself and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great men exercise authority over them. It is not this way among you, but whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave;

lines.text: Jesus is not scolding; He is describing how the world works. Everyone grew up watching the Gentiles install kings, generals and tetrarchs like Herod.

Perhaps James and John heard about the twelve thrones in 19:28, got excited and started planning: who sits on the right and the left? They missed that Jesus speaks in pictures of something spiritually deeper.

left.text: just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many.”

right.text: As a result of the anguish of His soul, / He will see it and be satisfied; / By His knowledge the Righteous One, / My Servant, will justify the many, / As He will bear their iniquities.

lines.text: 'A ransom for many' echoes the suffering servant who makes many righteous and bears their iniquities. This is intercessory language, and Isaiah 52-53 stands behind what Jesus says.
Isaiah 53:12 adds that He 'bore the sin of many, / And interceded for the transgressors.'

left.text: And He said to her, “What do you wish?” She *said to Him, “Command that in Your kingdom these two sons of mine may sit one on Your right and one on Your left.”

right.text: And Jesus stopped and called them, and said, “What do you want Me to do for you?”

lines.text: It is no coincidence that Jesus heals two blind men right after correcting two blind disciples. He asks both the same question, on purpose, so we connect them.
In Greek both questions use the same verb, thelō (to want, wish), though the LSB renders them 'wish' and 'want.'
The blind men call Him 'Son of David' and, once healed, follow Him (20:30, 34), while the crowd tries to silence them.

src.text: (Now this expression, “He ascended,” what does it mean except that He also descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is Himself also He who ascended far above all the heavens, so that He might fill all things.)

lines.text: Daniel saw only the ascension. Paul shows the real trajectory: ascension and glorification come after descending. That is the model for anyone who follows Christ.
Many in the church act like functional atheists: affirming the supernatural on Sunday and living by the world's system the rest of the week. That is likely why the rich young ruler walked away.

TERMS.def: The Jewish high council in Jerusalem, chief priests, elders and scribes.
A picture of God's wrath and of a God-given portion or destiny.
Greek lytron, the price paid to set someone free (20:28).
The servant of Isaiah 52:13-53:12, who suffers for many.

WORDS.gloss: Cup; in the Bible also one's lot, or God's wrath.
Ransom, the price of release. Look up: BDAG, λύτρον.
To want, wish: the verb of both questions.

BACKGROUND.p: Pilgrims from Galilee often crossed to the east bank, came south through Perea, recrossed near Jericho and climbed the steep road to Jerusalem, about 25 km and roughly 1,000 m of climb. Passover crowds would explain the large crowd in 20:29.
Under Roman rule the council could try cases, but capital sentences needed the governor, as John 18:31 states. So the prediction has two steps: the leaders condemn, the Gentiles execute.
In Psalm 110:1 the king sits at Yahweh's right hand, and in Psalm 16:11 pleasures are at His right hand. The places beside a king were the highest honors at court.

DEBATES.p: Some read John 19:25 as four women, making 'His mother's sister' Salome and the mother of the sons of Zebedee; others read three women, with the sister being Mary the wife of Clopas. The video presents the first as a possibility.
Early writers asked who received the ransom; most readers today take the word as a picture of release at great cost, echoing Isaiah 53, without pressing the question.
Jesus promised twelve thrones (19:28) yet refuses the right and left. Many see no conflict: the thrones are real, but the way to them is the cup.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The prediction of mocking, flogging and crucifixion is Matthew 20:18-19; the video once says 28:18-19.
The women at the cross in John are in John 19:25, not 19:2.
Early on the video says Jesus repeats the lesson from 20:6; the closest earlier statement is 'the last shall be first' (20:16) and the teaching on greatness in 18:1-4.
Saying that Hebrew has few words, so each word carries many meanings, is a generalization; the cup's two senses come mostly from how the image is used in different passages.
The LSB says 'betrayed' in 20:18 where the video's translation reads delivered over, and 'What do you wish?' in 20:21; the Greek verb is the same in 20:21 and 20:32.
Caption spellings: 'fgged' is flogged, 'rayim' is remazim (hints), 'for Ezra' is 4 Ezra, and 'Isaiah 52 and 253' is Isaiah 52 and 53.

QUESTIONS: Why might James and John have sent their mother rather than asking themselves?
What does 'the cup' mean in 20:22, and in what sense will they drink it (20:23)?
Why would Daniel 7 alone have left the disciples confused about a suffering Son of Man?
Where do you see the world's model of greatness creeping into church life?
What would it look like this week to 'descend' before you hope to 'ascend'?
If Jesus asked you, 'What do you want Me to do for you?', what would you say?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson: greatness in the kingdom of God is not based on the world's model of self-aggrandizement, but on Jesus' model of self-sacrifice. The cup that a Christian drinks will not be made of the world's gold, but of Christ's suffering. This is hard for anyone trained to see with physical eyes and steeped in the world's system; many in the church act like functional atheists. The path of Jesus is not a straight line of rising glory: He descended before He ascended. In the kingdom of heaven, those who seek self-denial and self-sacrifice are the ones God considers great. The cup before the crown, the cross before the throne.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): choose one hidden act of service this week that no one will thank you for, and before you do it, pray Philippians 2:5: have this attitude in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.

## Summary (from the video)

The ten are indignant, and Jesus teaches that the great among them must be servants, as the Son of Man came to serve and give His life a ransom for many. - Jesus has been travelling toward Jerusalem since 19:1. 'Chief priests and scribes' with the power to condemn points to the Sanhedrin, which then handed people to Rome for execution. Jesus speaks of His death as 'the Son of Man,' the figure of Daniel 7:13-14.
- The mother speaks, but Jesus answers the sons, who answer back: they had put her up to it. The video suggests she may have been Mary's sister, which would make James and John Jesus' cousins. ## The Son of Man will be handed over
1. Matthew 20:17-19: Going up to Jerusalem

2. Matthew 20:18; John 18:31: Chief priests and scribes
   Jesus (Matthew 20:18, LSB): "“Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem; and the Son of Man will be betrayed to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn Him to death,"

3. Daniel 7:13-14: The Son of Man
   Remez Daniel 7:13-14: "“I kept looking in the night visions, / And behold, with the clouds of heaven / One like a Son of Man was coming, / And He came up to the Ancient of Days / And came near before Him. / And to Him was given dominion, / Glory, and a kingdom, / That all the peoples, nations, and men of every tongue / Might serve Him. / His dominion is an everlasting dominion / Which will not be taken away; / And His kingdom is one / Which will not be destroyed." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Daniel+7:13-14
   (video) Jesus does not say 'I will die' in 20:18; He uses 'the Son of Man,' pointing to Old Testament prophecy about the Messiah. None of this should have surprised the disciples.
   (video) Other texts outside the Bible, including 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra, probably shaped expectations too. But Daniel never saw the Son of Man suffer and die, and that probably confused the disciples.
4. Isaiah 53:3-5; 52:14: Despised and forsaken
   Suffering servant Isaiah 53:3-5: "He was despised and forsaken of men, / A man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; / And like one from whom men hide their face / He was despised, and we did not esteem Him. / Surely our griefs He Himself bore, / And our sorrows He carried; / Yet we ourselves esteemed Him stricken, / Smitten of God, and afflicted. / But He was pierced through for our transgressions, / He was crushed for our iniquities; / The chastening for our peace fell upon Him, / And by His wounds we are healed." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Isaiah+53:3-5
   (video) Where does Jesus get the mocking and flogging? From Isaiah 52 and 53, where the servant is oppressed, afflicted, pierced, His appearance marred more than any man (52:14; 53:7). (Isaiah 52:14; Isaiah 53:7)
   (video) The disciples should have known Daniel 7 and Isaiah 52-53. It seems they missed these hints.

## Are you able to drink the cup?
1. Matthew 20:20-22: Who is asking?
   The mother (Matthew 20:21, LSB): "And He said to her, “What do you wish?” She *said to Him, “Command that in Your kingdom these two sons of mine may sit one on Your right and one on Your left.”"
   Jesus to the sons (Matthew 20:22, LSB): "But Jesus answered and said, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?” They *said to Him, “We are able.”"
   (video) She asks, but Jesus does not answer her. He speaks straight to James and John, and they answer Him. They had put their mother up to it.
   [Background] Mark 10:35-37 tells it with James and John making the request themselves. (Mark 10:35-37)
2. Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56; John 19:25: Jesus' aunt?
   Possible Matthew 27:56: "Among them was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+27:56
   (video) Comparing the women at the cross, she could have been Mary's sister, Jesus' aunt. That would make James and John His cousins, and her appeal makes more sense: she wants His family to have royal recognition.
   [Background] Mark names Salome at the cross (Mark 15:40); John names His mother's sister (John 19:25). Whether these are the same woman is an inference, not stated. (Mark 15:40; John 19:25)
3. Jeremiah 25:15; Isaiah 51:17; Matthew 26:39: The cup of wrath
   Yahweh to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 25:15, LSB): "For thus Yahweh, the God of Israel, says to me, “Take this cup of the wine of wrath from My hand and cause all the nations to whom I send you to drink it."
   Jesus in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39, LSB): "And He went a little beyond them, and fell on His face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; yet not as I will, but as You will.”"
   (video) The cup is a common picture of suffering, especially the suffering caused by God's wrath. Isaiah 51:17 speaks of Jerusalem drinking the cup of His wrath, and Jesus will pray in Gethsemane for this cup to pass. (Isaiah 51:17)
   (video) So the rhetorical answer to 'Are you able?' is no: only Jesus can drink the cup of God's wrath and take on the sins of the whole world.
4. Psalm 16:5; Matthew 20:23: My portion and my cup
   David (Psalm 16:5, LSB): "Yahweh is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; / You support my lot."
   Jesus (Matthew 20:23, LSB): "He *said to them, “My cup you shall drink; but to sit on My right and on My left, this is not Mine to give, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by My Father.”"
   (video) The cup is also a person's God-given portion or destiny. In that sense Jesus can say 'My cup you shall drink': they will share His rejection, persecution and self-denial, and His obedience unto glory.
   (video) And He was right. James is killed by Herod (Acts 12:2) and John suffers exile on Patmos (Revelation 1:9). (Acts 12:2; Revelation 1:9)
   (video) Jesus is a servant of the Father's will; all authority is given to Him later (28:18). As He yields to the Father, James and John should let go of their desire for authority.

## Whoever wishes to become great
1. Matthew 20:24-27: Not this way among you
   Greatness Matthew 20:25-27: "But Jesus called them to Himself and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great men exercise authority over them. It is not this way among you, but whoever wishes to become great among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave;" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+20:25-27
   (video) Jesus is not scolding; He is describing how the world works. Everyone grew up watching the Gentiles install kings, generals and tetrarchs like Herod.
   (video) Perhaps James and John heard about the twelve thrones in 19:28, got excited and started planning: who sits on the right and the left? They missed that Jesus speaks in pictures of something spiritually deeper. (Matthew 19:28)
2. Matthew 20:28; Isaiah 53:11-12: A ransom for many
   Jesus (Matthew 20:28, LSB): "just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many.”"
   Isaiah (Isaiah 53:11, LSB): "As a result of the anguish of His soul, / He will see it and be satisfied; / By His knowledge the Righteous One, / My Servant, will justify the many, / As He will bear their iniquities."
   (video) 'A ransom for many' echoes the suffering servant who makes many righteous and bears their iniquities. This is intercessory language, and Isaiah 52-53 stands behind what Jesus says.
   [Background] Isaiah 53:12 adds that He 'bore the sin of many, / And interceded for the transgressors.'
3. Matthew 20:21, 32: What do you want?
   Jesus to the mother (Matthew 20:21, LSB): "And He said to her, “What do you wish?” She *said to Him, “Command that in Your kingdom these two sons of mine may sit one on Your right and one on Your left.”"
   Jesus to the blind men (Matthew 20:32, LSB): "And Jesus stopped and called them, and said, “What do you want Me to do for you?”"
   (video) It is no coincidence that Jesus heals two blind men right after correcting two blind disciples. He asks both the same question, on purpose, so we connect them.
   [Background] In Greek both questions use the same verb, thelō (to want, wish), though the LSB renders them 'wish' and 'want.'
   [Background] The blind men call Him 'Son of David' and, once healed, follow Him (20:30, 34), while the crowd tries to silence them. (Matthew 20:30; Matthew 20:34)
4. Ephesians 4:9-10: Descended, then ascended
   Lesson Ephesians 4:9-10: "(Now this expression, “He ascended,” what does it mean except that He also descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is Himself also He who ascended far above all the heavens, so that He might fill all things.)" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Ephesians+4:9-10
   (video) Daniel saw only the ascension. Paul shows the real trajectory: ascension and glorification come after descending. That is the model for anyone who follows Christ.
   (video) Many in the church act like functional atheists: affirming the supernatural on Sunday and living by the world's system the rest of the week. That is likely why the rich young ruler walked away.

## Key people
- The Son of Man: Jesus' name for Himself as He predicts His death and rising. [Background] The figure of Daniel 7:13-14, who receives an everlasting dominion.
- The mother of the sons of Zebedee: Kneels and asks for the places at His right and left; perhaps Mary's sister. [Background] She is at the cross in 27:56; Mark 15:40 names Salome there.
- James and John: Put their mother up to it; say 'We are able.' [Background] James is killed by Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:2); John is exiled on Patmos (Revelation 1:9).
- The ten: Indignant at the two brothers. [Background] Jesus calls all twelve and teaches them together (20:25).
- The two blind men: Cry out for mercy; their healing mirrors the disciples' blindness. [Background] Mark 10:46 and Luke 18:35 tell of one blind man; Mark names him Bartimaeus.

## Places [Background]
- Perea: 'Judea beyond the Jordan' (19:1), the road south.
- Jericho (named in the video): 'As they were leaving Jericho' (20:29): the two blind men.
- Jerusalem (named in the video): 'We are going up to Jerusalem' (20:18).

## Key terms
- Son of Man: Jesus' favorite self-title, from Daniel 7:13-14.
- Sanhedrin: The Jewish high council in Jerusalem, chief priests, elders and scribes.
- Cup: A picture of God's wrath and of a God-given portion or destiny.
- Ransom: Greek lytron, the price paid to set someone free (20:28). [Background]
- Suffering servant: The servant of Isaiah 52:13-53:12, who suffers for many.
- Remez: A hint: a phrase that points back to a whole Old Testament passage.

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- The road from Jericho: Pilgrims from Galilee often crossed to the east bank, came south through Perea, recrossed near Jericho and climbed the steep road to Jerusalem, about 25 km and roughly 1,000 m of climb. Passover crowds would explain the large crowd in 20:29.
- The Sanhedrin's limits: Under Roman rule the council could try cases, but capital sentences needed the governor, as John 18:31 states. So the prediction has two steps: the leaders condemn, the Gentiles execute.
- Right hand and left: In Psalm 110:1 the king sits at Yahweh's right hand, and in Psalm 16:11 pleasures are at His right hand. The places beside a king were the highest honors at court.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Was she Jesus' aunt? Some read John 19:25 as four women, making 'His mother's sister' Salome and the mother of the sons of Zebedee; others read three women, with the sister being Mary the wife of Clopas. The video presents the first as a possibility.
- Ransom paid to whom? Early writers asked who received the ransom; most readers today take the word as a picture of release at great cost, echoing Isaiah 53, without pressing the question.
- Thrones and a cup Jesus promised twelve thrones (19:28) yet refuses the right and left. Many see no conflict: the thrones are real, but the way to them is the cup.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The prediction of mocking, flogging and crucifixion is Matthew 20:18-19; the video once says 28:18-19.
- The women at the cross in John are in John 19:25, not 19:2.
- Early on the video says Jesus repeats the lesson from 20:6; the closest earlier statement is 'the last shall be first' (20:16) and the teaching on greatness in 18:1-4.
- Saying that Hebrew has few words, so each word carries many meanings, is a generalization; the cup's two senses come mostly from how the image is used in different passages.
- The LSB says 'betrayed' in 20:18 where the video's translation reads delivered over, and 'What do you wish?' in 20:21; the Greek verb is the same in 20:21 and 20:32.
- Caption spellings: 'fgged' is flogged, 'rayim' is remazim (hints), 'for Ezra' is 4 Ezra, and 'Isaiah 52 and 253' is Isaiah 52 and 53.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why might James and John have sent their mother rather than asking themselves?
2. What does 'the cup' mean in 20:22, and in what sense will they drink it (20:23)?
3. Why would Daniel 7 alone have left the disciples confused about a suffering Son of Man?
4. Where do you see the world's model of greatness creeping into church life?
5. What would it look like this week to 'descend' before you hope to 'ascend'?
6. If Jesus asked you, 'What do you want Me to do for you?', what would you say?

## Application
- (video) The lesson: greatness in the kingdom of God is not based on the world's model of self-aggrandizement, but on Jesus' model of self-sacrifice. The cup that a Christian drinks will not be made of the world's gold, but of Christ's suffering. This is hard for anyone trained to see with physical eyes and steeped in the world's system; many in the church act like functional atheists. The path of Jesus is not a straight line of rising glory: He descended before He ascended. In the kingdom of heaven, those who seek self-denial and self-sacrifice are the ones God considers great. The cup before the crown, the cross before the throne.
- Study note (added): choose one hidden act of service this week that no one will thank you for, and before you do it, pray Philippians 2:5: have this attitude in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.
